en: The Sūtra on the Elder’s Pleasing Voice, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, together with his honored [assembly].

Accompanied by his twelve hundred and fifty disciples, as well as various bodhisattvas, laymen, and laywomen—all assembled together in a great gathering surrounding him as he preached the Dharma—the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"There was a householder named Ghoṣadatta, whose wealth was beyond counting. Being advanced in years and childless, he was filled with grief and sorrow."
Although this was so, it was pursued by the merit of past lives, and its rewards were fourfold:
first, the lady gave birth to a son of incomparable and upright beauty;
second, five hundred white horses simultaneously gave birth to foals.
"Third, a king shall dispatch an envoy to confer upon him a golden seal;
fourth, five hundred precious ships shall arrive simultaneously.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“What kind of precious ships have all arrived together?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The merchant’s clan was exceedingly numerous. Prior to this time, he had dispatched five hundred men to enter the sea by ship; having obtained a multitude of treasures, they returned home in safety.”
"Therefore, the Tathāgata says that these four blessings converge simultaneously and universally.
The elder was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"Heaven has sent down blessings upon my courtyard; I shall prepare sweet delicacies so that my household and kin may celebrate together."
He then acted according to those words and established a great kitchen.
All enjoyed themselves to the full; the sounds of drums, music, strings, and song reached the heavens.

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra and Brahmā, the various dragon kings, ghost kings, asura kings, and all the spirit kings, each accompanied by their retinues, filled the void of space to witness the immeasurable merit of this elder.
The Tathāgata, possessing divine penetration, knew that this elder was leaping with joy.
Because of his gladness, he wished to go and praise him, thinking that if he were to attain understanding, he could plant the seeds of merit.
The Tathāgata, at that opportune moment, sang the auspicious verses of the eight sounds and went outside the gate, where he spoke these stanzas:
"Today for the elder, Auspiciousness has gathered; All blessings have responded, And the entire household is blessed with prosperity."
Great and small alike are filled with joy; there is nothing in the world to compare with this.
All the devas, nāgas, and spirits have been brought to submission. How wonderful, O Elder!
"Just as when one sows grain in spring, it ripens in autumn; so too, having acted first, one receives later—the shadow of retribution follows.
At that time, the elder, hearing the Buddha’s virtuous voice, felt his five senses filled with ease and departed in great joy.
Beholding the Buddha with reverent solemnity, he immediately addressed him, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama is truly divine and wondrous!
You know that my family lineage possesses immeasurable auspiciousness."
"Please condescend to honor us by coming to offer your praise.
He then presented to the Tathāgata fine white cotton cloth worth ten million taels of gold.
The Buddha accepted it and bestowed a *dakṣiṇā* (blessing) upon him.
The Buddha told the householder:
"There are five perils of wealth that people of the world do not recognize; being stingy, parsimonious, and greedy, they are unable to diminish or cut their own portion to provide for the destitute."
"When life ends and the spirit departs, one leaves behind all worldly wealth.
Since you are now able to act thus, you will surely obtain a karmic reward; wherever you are reborn, blessings shall naturally attend you."
The householder addressed the Buddha,
"What are the five dangers?
The Buddha then replied:
"First, it is not perceived when burned by a great fire;
second, it is swept away and lost in the impermanence of great waters;
third, it is seized by officials through unrighteous means."
Fourth, evil children spend beyond all limits;
fifth, they are plundered by robbers and thieves.

When any one of these five things occurs, it cannot be restrained. It is like a person who violates the royal law, is cast into prison, and ought to be executed, with his property confiscated by the government; how could he possibly turn back such a fate?
Furthermore, it is like Anāthapiṇḍika, whose countless treasures were seized by a king; the owner could not restrain him, nor was he able to stop him even through divine dragons.
"Why is this? Because in his previous lives he gave alms seven times and then regretted them; therefore, in this present life, he has been wealthy seven times and poor seven times.
When the elder heard this teaching, his joy increased all the more.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata suddenly returned to Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, there was a heterodox practitioner of the Nirgrantha school in the kingdom named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. Having heard that the Tathāgata had visited the house of the elder, recited a single verse of praise, and unworthily obtained ten million taels of gold from the elder, he harbored feelings of resentment and jealousy. He thought to himself:
"If even the śramaṇa Gautama can obtain gold, how much more so should I be able to obtain it by going to beg for it?"
He further thought to himself:
"I shall go to seek the verse spoken by the śramaṇa Gautama; only then will I go to beg, and I will surely obtain precious jewels."
"It would be more fitting to praise him; he should indeed surpass Gautama.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, harboring such foolishness and envy, went to pay his respects to the Tathāgata. He knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am of meager virtue and without merit; my food and clothing are not sufficient."
"I have heard that Gautama visited the house of the elder and obtained a great quantity of precious treasures by reciting a single verse.
Would you not deign to show me compassion and grant me the verse he spoke, so that I may commit it to memory?"
"You should go there to offer praise, hoping to obtain treasure.

The Tathāgata, possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge, knew that at a later time this elder’s wealth would be dispersed; he also knew that Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, being ignorant of the proper timing, would encounter a family in distress and yet preach words of auspiciousness, thereby inevitably causing the elder immeasurable suffering from blows with a staff.
The Tathāgata replied:
"I do not begrudge this verse. Why is that? "
"You do not know the proper time.
If you recite these verses, you will surely suffer severe punishment; therefore, the Tathāgata has declined your request.
If you desire further timely discourse and exquisite phrases, I shall grant them to you, so that the elder may hear the true words and you yourself may be spared the agony of the flogging."
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama does not wish for me to go and beg for precious jewels; that is why he is being stingy and refuses to give them to me."
He then addressed him once more:
"As for what he has given me, how could I know anything else?
Out of compassion, the Tathāgata admonished him up to three times, yet in the end, he remained without faith or understanding.
The Buddha also foresaw in advance that,
due to the karmic conditions of his previous lives, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was destined to undergo this suffering.
The Tathāgata further said:
"Sin cannot be repaid.
The Buddha then recited for him verses of auspiciousness.
The Nirgrantha chanted them until, after one year, he had mastered them by heart.
Thereafter, a fire broke out in the elder’s house and all his rare treasures were consumed;
five hundred foals died simultaneously in the flames;
and the wonderful son he had begotten perished in a single day.
The king dispatched a messenger to confiscate his golden seal.

Later, he again boarded a ship to enter the sea to gather treasures; having returned safely, he anchored at the shore for several days, when five hundred treasure ships suddenly drifted away and sank.

Everyone in the household, both great and small, was filled with grief and distress; it was as if someone had been sentenced to execution, where the sorrow and terror in the moments before death are beyond words.
On that day, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa went to his gate and sang these verses on the auspiciousness of the Tathāgata:
"Today for the elder, Auspiciousness has gathered; All blessings and responses Have come together."
The family clan prospers with good fortune;
great and small alike are filled with joy. There is nothing in the world to compare with this;
all the devas, nāgas, and spirits are brought to submission.
How joyous is the elder!
Just as grain sown in spring ripens in autumn, so too does one first act and later receive the fruit;
the shadow of retribution follows closely behind.
When Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa spoke this verse, the elder heard it and, with his head raised in indignation, cried out:
"In all the world, no one is more wretched or calamity-stricken than I!"
"How can this person, naked and shameless, utter propitious words for me here amidst such demonic sorcery, only to increase my distress?
He immediately went out and beat him, inflicting suffering from head to foot.
His entire body was in great pain, and he crawled back home.
The six heretical teachers and their followers met him and asked about his intentions.
He replied:
"This transformation is surely due to Gautama.
Not examining his own internal failings, he instead harbored resentment toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, surrounded by a great assembly, preaching the Dharma.
The Buddha addressed the assembly:
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa previously requested a verse from the Tathāgata, desiring to go to an elder to recite it in hopes of obtaining treasures.
The Tathāgata admonished him, yet he remained in disbelief."
"He is already there, suffering from agonizing pain.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"What karmic connection did Pūraṇa Kāśyapa have with this householder that he has been stricken by such an affliction?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a king whose name was also Ruciraghoṣa."
Furthermore, there was another bird named Śuka (Parrot) perched above the royal palace, its call melodious and harmonious.
While the king was napping during the day, he was startled awake by the sound of the bird's cry and asked his attendants,
"What kind of bird is this, whose song is so exquisite?"
The attendant replied, "There was a marvelous bird, resplendent with five colors, which was just now above the palace; having called out, it departed.
The king immediately dispatched a great multitude, with infantry and cavalry streaming forth in succession, to pursue and seek it.
After searching for a very long time, he captured it and presented it to the king.

The king was filled with joy; his delight was such that he could never tire of it. He immediately adorned its body with necklaces of pearls, crystal, lapis lazuli, and genuine pearls, as well as coral, covering its head, neck, and wings without exception.
He kept it constantly by his side, gazing upon it day and night, not departing from it for even a moment.
"Later, there was another bird named the Bald Owl that came and perched atop the palace.
Seeing that the parrot alone had received such exceptional favor, it asked the parrot:
'By what cause have you attained this? "

The parrot replied, "I came to perch upon the palace and sang with a most beautiful and mournful cry; the king loved and respected me, so he took me and kept me constantly by his side, adorning my body with necklaces of five-colored pearls and jewels."
When the bald owl heard this, he harbored jealousy in his heart and thought to himself:
"I too shall cry out, so as to surpass you;
the king shall likewise love and favor my person."
At that time, as the king went out to lie down, a bald owl immediately cried out. The king was instantly startled awake; his hair stood on end, and he appeared as if struck with terror.
The king asked those around him, "What is this sound that has so startled and terrified me?"
The attendant replied,
"There is a bird of ill omen called the *kroñca*.
The king then spoke in anger:
"Quickly dispatch the great multitude to search for him everywhere!
They immediately found him and presented him to the king.
The king ordered his attendants to pluck out the feathers from his body by force; suffering intense pain throughout his entire frame, he departed on foot.
Upon reaching that wild field, the various birds asked him,
"For what reason have you come here?
The bald owl, filled with resentment and failing to blame himself, replied to the birds:
"Because this parrot spoke correctly, it has incurred this calamity.
The Buddha said, "A good voice invites blessings, while an evil voice brings disaster. Since the retribution for one's sins originates with oneself, you instead turn your anger upon the parrot."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The king of old was this Elder Svarasena;
the parrot was my own self."
The bald owl was none other than Pūraṇa Kāśyapa in his present life.
In the past, out of jealousy toward the parrot, he suffered the calamity of poison;
now, out of jealousy toward the Tathāgata, he has incurred unspeakable agony.
Greed and envy burn the body; how much more so when faced with suffering and hardship? Why is this?
Because Pūraṇa Kāśyapa slandered the Tathāgata on six occasions, both before and after.
What are these six?
First, being in a difficult land, they give rise to greed and envy, slandering the Tathāgata;
second, in Rājagṛha, for the sake of the Bamboo Grove, they slander the Tathāgata.
Third, while in Rājagṛha, he went to the house of the elder Ghosila, coveting his gold and jewels, and slandered the Tathāgata;
fourth, within the realm of Magadha, he coveted offerings and slandered the Tathāgata;
fifth, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, he coveted fame and material gain, and slandered the Tathāgata.
Sixth, while in Śrāvastī, he was greedy for gain and offerings and begrudged his reputation; consequently, he slandered the Tathāgata.
At that time, the king banished him from the country.
The six teachers, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and his disciples, spoke with one mind, saying:
"Gautama is truly a divine being; there is none who does not revere him.
Our own arts are shallow, our reputations have collapsed, and we are everywhere treated with contempt. What is the use of living on?"

Immediately, he placed sand inside a bottle and submerged it himself in the water; thereupon his life came to an end, and he entered hell, where he was subjected to all manner of tortures and immeasurable suffering.
The Buddha spoke again:

"In future ages, there will be many people who are greedy, envious, depraved, and evil; they will slander others, be arrogant, and seek out each other's faults. This is truly self-immolation and suffering."
“Ānanda!
For this reason, you should widely proclaim this sutra in order to protect such followers in the future.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“What merit did the householder Svaramadhura plant in the past to obtain these four blessings?
What misdeeds did he commit that caused him to lose them?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In his previous life, when Yueyin was a youth, he revered the Buddha-dharma and the assembly of noble ones; he made offerings with utmost devotion and prayed for wealth and status.

However, after taking a wife, he became exclusively infatuated with sensual forms, showing neglect and arrogance toward the Triple Gem, and lacked the compassionate heart to treat elders and juniors with kindness."
"Therefore, once the retribution has been fully exhausted, one immediately disperses.
You must provide guidance and proclaim this, so that they may understand its essential point.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and commoners—all those gathered there—heard the sutra with joy; there were none who did not prostrate themselves in worship.
The Sūtra on the Elder’s Melodious Voice Spoken by the Buddha
